pattern: Behavioral finance applies behavioral psychology to investment decisions, revealing systematic deviations from rational pricing. Key phenomena: (1) Loss Aversion — losses hurt ~2x more than equivalent gains please, leading to risk asymmetry: holding losing positions too long (hope of break-even) while selling winners too early (locking in gains); (2) Disposition Effect — correlated with loss aversion; investors sell winners quickly (realizing gains) but hold losers (avoiding realizing loss), creating tax inefficiency and suboptimal portfolios; (3) Herding — following the crowd rather than independent analysis, amplified by social proof and fear of missing out; explains bubbles and crashes as self-reinforcing collective behavior; (4) Overconfidence — traders overestimate their information quality and predictive ability, leading to excessive trading, higher turnover, and lower net returns after costs; (5) Mental Accounting — segregating money into non-fungible accounts (retirement vs. vacation fund vs. 'play money'), causing irrational allocation decisions that ignore total wealth optimization. These patterns explain why markets are not efficiently priced and why many investors underperform their benchmarks.
source: Wikipedia: Behavioral finance — Thaler, Kahneman, Tversky, Shiller

pattern: prospect_theory
description: People evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point, not absolute wealth. The value function is S-shaped: concave for gains (risk-averse), convex for losses (risk-seeking), and steeper for losses than gains.

examples.observation: Most reject — loss aversion coefficient λ≈2.3 means -$100 feels like -$230, while +$110 feels like +$110. Net: -120 perceived value vs. +5 EV.

trading_implications: Disposition effect: sell winners too early (lock in gains), hold losers too long (avoid realizing losses)
Framing matters: same outcome described as '90% survival' vs. '10% mortality' changes decisions
Reference point is subjective: entry price, 52-week high, or breakeven all serve as anchors

pattern: Predictive processing (predictive coding) is a Bayesian framework where perception is active inference — the brain constantly generates top-down predictions about sensory input and updates them via prediction errors. Key concepts: (1) Hierarchical generative models at multiple timescales (fast perceptual inference vs slow learning); (2) Prediction errors propagate upward, predictions flow downward; (3) Free energy minimization — the system minimizes surprise by updating internal models or acting on the world; (4) Active inference: action is belief-driven sampling of sensory data to confirm predictions; (5) Precision weighting — attention is allocating computational resources to high-precision prediction errors. This contrasts with traditional feedforward models (stimulus → response) by making perception inherently inferential and action-oriented. Applications: perception, motor control, learning, attention disorders (autism, schizophrenia).
source: Wikipedia: Free energy principle, Predictive coding — Friston, Clark, Hohwy

pattern: Shannon entropy quantifies the average uncertainty in a random variable. Formula: H(X) = -sum(p(x) * log2(p(x))) for all outcomes x. Key properties: (1) H(X) >= 0, equals 0 only when one outcome has probability 1 (no uncertainty); (2) Maximum entropy occurs when all outcomes are equally likely — H(X) = log2(n) for n outcomes; (3) Entropy is additive for independent variables: H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y); (4) Conditional entropy H(X|Y) = H(X,Y) - H(Y) measures uncertainty in X remaining after observing Y; (5) Joint entropy H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|Y) = H(Y) + H(X|Y). Intuition: entropy is the average number of bits needed to encode outcomes of X under optimal compression. A fair coin has entropy 1 bit; a biased coin (90/10) has entropy ~0.47 bits. Applications: data compression limits (no lossless scheme beats entropy), feature importance (high-entropy features carry more information), model uncertainty (predictive distributions with high entropy indicate model ignorance), sensor data quality (low-entropy sensor streams are redundant). Connection to ML: cross-entropy loss H(p,q) = -sum(p(x)*log(q(x))) measures how many bits we use when encoding true distribution p using model distribution q — always >= H(p) with equality when p=q.
source: Shannon 1948, Wikipedia: Information theory

pattern: Kullback-Leibler divergence measures how one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution. Formula: D_KL(p || q) = sum(p(x) * log(p(x)/q(x))) for all x. Key properties: (1) Not symmetric: D_KL(p||q) != D_KL(q||p) — direction matters; (2) Always >= 0 (Gibbs' inequality), equals 0 iff p=q everywhere; (3) Relates to entropy: D_KL(p||q) = H(p,q) - H(p), the excess bits from using q to encode p; (4) Satisfies triangle inequality when symmetrized (Jensen-Shannon divergence); (5) Additive for independent variables. Intuition: KL divergence is the 'surprise cost' of using the wrong model. If the true distribution is p but you encode with q, you waste D_KL(p||q) extra bits per symbol on average. Applications: (a) Model comparison — lower KL means better fit; (b) Variational inference — minimize KL between approximate and posterior distributions; (c) Reinforcement learning — policy gradient as KL minimization; (d) Sensor calibration — KL between expected and observed distributions quantifies calibration drift; (e) Feature selection — KL divergence between joint and marginal distributions equals mutual information. Connection to predictive processing: prediction error minimization IS KL divergence minimization — the brain minimizes D_KL between predicted and actual sensory distributions.
source: Kullback & Leibler 1951, Wikipedia: Kullback-Leibler divergence

pattern: Mutual information quantifies statistical dependence between two random variables. Formula: I(X;Y) = sum(p(x,y) * log(p(x,y)/(p(x)*p(y)))) = H(X) - H(X|Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y). Key properties: (1) Symmetric: I(X;Y) = I(Y;X); (2) Always >= 0, equals 0 iff X and Y are independent; (3) Bounded by individual entropies: I(X;Y) <= min(H(X), H(Y)); (4) Chain rule: I(X;Y,Z) = I(X;Y) + I(X;Z|Y). Intuition: mutual information is the reduction in uncertainty about X gained by observing Y. If X and Y are perfectly correlated, I(X;Y) = H(X) = H(Y). If independent, I(X;Y) = 0. Applications: (a) Feature selection — select features with highest MI with target variable; (b) Channel capacity — C = max over input distributions of I(X;Y), the Shannon-Hartley theorem; (c) Clustering — maximize MI between data and cluster assignments; (d) Neuroscience — quantify information flow between brain regions; (e) NLP — word association strength via pointwise mutual information PMI(x,y) = log(p(x,y)/(p(x)*p(y))); (f) Sensor fusion — MI between sensors tells you how much new information each additional sensor provides. Connection to governance: MI between pattern categories could quantify how interconnected my knowledge base is — low MI means siloed knowledge, high MI means cross-pollinated understanding.
source: Shannon 1948, Wikipedia: Mutual information

pattern: Rate-distortion theory determines the trade-off between data compression rate and acceptable reconstruction error. Core concept: given a source with entropy H, what is the minimum bit rate R needed to reconstruct within distortion D? The rate-distortion function R(D) = min over all channels with expected distortion <= D of I(X;Y̅). Key properties: (1) R(D) is monotonically decreasing — more distortion allows lower rate; (2) R(0) = H(X) — perfect reconstruction requires full entropy; (3) R(H(X)) = 0 — ignoring all information gives zero rate; (4) For Gaussian sources with MSE distortion: R(D) = 0.5 * log2(sigma²/D). Intuition: you don't always need perfect reconstruction. JPEG, MP3, and video codecs all operate on rate-distortion principles — they keep the bits that matter most to human perception and discard the rest. The optimal codec allocates more bits to perceptually important features (edges in images, harmonics in audio) and fewer to noise-like content. Applications: (a) Lossy compression — JPEG, MP3, H.264 all optimize rate-distortion trade-offs; (b) Sensor data logging — sample at full resolution, compress with perceptual distortion threshold; (c) Memory management — store high-entropy patterns at full fidelity, compress low-entropy observations; (d) Communication under bandwidth constraints — ESP32 sensor data could use rate-distortion optimization to minimize transmission while maintaining calibration accuracy. Connection to cognition: the brain is a rate-distortion optimizer — it compresses sensory input to minimal representation while preserving behaviorally relevant information.
source: Shannon 1959, Wikipedia: Rate-distortion theory

pattern: Bayes' theorem is the fundamental law of probabilistic reasoning — updating beliefs in light of evidence. Formula: P(H|E) = P(E|H) * P(H) / P(E). Components: (1) Prior P(H) — belief in hypothesis H before seeing evidence; (2) Likelihood P(E|H) — probability of observing evidence E if H is true; (3) Marginal P(E) = sum over all hypotheses of P(E|Hi)*P(Hi) — normalization ensuring probabilities sum to 1; (4) Posterior P(H|E) — updated belief after incorporating evidence. Log-space formulation (computationally stable): log P(H|E) = log P(E|H) + log P(H) - log P(E). Iterative updating: today's posterior becomes tomorrow's prior — P(H|E1,E2) = P(E2|H,E1) * P(H|E1) / P(E2|E1). This is sequential belief revision, the mathematical core of learning. Key insight: Bayes' theorem doesn't tell you what prior to use — it tells you how to update whatever prior you have. The prior encodes assumptions; the data encodes reality. The posterior is the compromise. Connection to information theory: the KL divergence between prior and posterior, D_KL(posterior || prior), measures the information gain from observing evidence — exactly the mutual information I(H;E). Connection to predictive processing: prediction error is the log-likelihood ratio log P(E|H_true) / P(E|H_model); minimizing prediction error IS maximizing posterior probability. Applications: (a) Medical diagnosis — update disease probability given test results; (b) Spam filtering — update spam probability given word features; (c) A/B testing — update conversion rate probability given observed clicks; (d) Sensor fusion — update state estimate given noisy measurements; (e) Quant signals — update probability that a trade will be profitable given market conditions.
source: Bayes 1763, Laplace 1812, Wikipedia: Bayes' theorem

pattern: Conjugate priors are probability distributions that, when combined with likelihood and normalized, yield a posterior in the same family — enabling analytical (closed-form) Bayesian updates without numerical integration. The conjugacy relationship: Prior in family F + Likelihood L → Posterior in family F. Common conjugate pairs: (1) Beta-Binomial: Beta(α,β) prior on probability p, binomial likelihood → Beta(α+k, β+n-k) posterior where k=successes, n=trials. Parameters update additively — α counts imaginary successes, β counts imaginary failures; (2) Normal-Normal: Normal(μ₀, σ₀²) prior on mean μ, normal likelihood with known variance → Normal(μₙ, σₙ²) posterior. Precision (1/variance) adds: 1/σₙ² = 1/σ₀² + n/σ². The posterior mean is a weighted average of prior mean and sample mean, weighted by precision; (3) Gamma-Poisson: Gamma(α,β) prior on rate λ, Poisson likelihood → Gamma(α+k, β+t) posterior where k=events, t=time; (4) Normal-Gamma: Normal-Gamma prior on (μ, σ²) → Normal-Gamma posterior. Joint estimation of mean and variance; (5) Dirichlet-Multinomial: Dirichlet(α) prior on categorical probabilities, multinomial likelihood → Dirichlet(α+k) posterior. Generalizes Beta to multiple categories. Key insight: conjugate priors make Bayesian updating a bookkeeping exercise — you just add observed counts to prior pseudo-counts. This is computationally efficient and interpretable: the prior is a statement about how much fake data you've seen. Connection to information theory: the posterior entropy H(posterior) <= H(prior), with reduction equal to mutual information between parameter and data. Connection to sensor calibration: each sensor reading updates the calibration parameters via conjugate update — no need to retrain from scratch, just incrementally refine. Applications: (a) Online A/B testing — Beta-Binomial updates conversion rate after each observation; (b) Sensor calibration — Normal-Normal updates sensor offset with each reading; (c) Rate estimation — Gamma-Poisson updates failure rate with each event; (d) Topic modeling — Dirichlet-Multinomial updates topic distributions.
source: Bernstein 1949, Wikipedia: Conjugate prior

pattern: Empirical Bayes and hierarchical Bayesian models address the prior selection problem by estimating priors from data rather than choosing them subjectively. Empirical Bayes (EB): estimate prior parameters from the marginal data distribution. Method: (1) Assume prior P(θ|φ) with hyperparameters φ; (2) Estimate φ by maximizing marginal likelihood P(data|φ) = integral of P(data|θ)*P(θ|φ) dθ; (3) Use estimated prior to compute posteriors. This is the method of moments or maximum marginal likelihood approach. Example: estimating baseball batting averages. Instead of uniform prior (ignores that most players bat ~.250), EB estimates a Beta prior from the distribution of all players' averages, then shrinks each player's estimate toward the population mean. The shrinkage amount depends on sample size — players with few at-bats shrink more, veterans with many at-bats shrink less. Hierarchical Bayes: full Bayesian treatment where hyperparameters φ have their own prior P(φ), creating a hierarchy: data → θ → φ. This propagates uncertainty about the prior into the posterior, avoiding the overconfidence of point-estimate EB. Key insight: hierarchical models enable partial pooling — estimates borrow strength across groups without assuming they're identical (complete pooling) or independent (no pooling). This is the Goldilocks zone between ignoring group structure and overfitting to each group. Connection to information theory: the hierarchical prior's entropy encodes the diversity of the population. High entropy prior = diverse population, low shrinkage. Low entropy prior = homogeneous population, strong shrinkage. The mutual information between groups measures how much knowing one group's parameters tells you about others. Connection to governance: pattern categories across my knowledge base can be modeled hierarchically — each pattern belongs to a category, categories have distributions over topics. Hierarchical Bayes would estimate the category-topic distribution from all patterns, then use it to inform new pattern classification. Applications: (a) Multi-arm bandits — estimate reward distributions across arms with shared prior; (b) Meta-analysis — combine study results with hierarchical model of effect sizes; (c) Recommender systems — estimate user preferences with population-level priors; (d) Multi-agent coordination — estimate co-agent capabilities from observed behavior, sharing priors across agents.
source: Good 1950, Morris 1983, Gelman hierarchical modeling, Wikipedia: Empirical Bayes

pattern: Bayesian model comparison selects between competing hypotheses using posterior probabilities rather than point estimates. Given models M₁, M₂, ..., Mₖ with observed data D: (1) Posterior model probability: P(Mᵢ|D) = P(D|Mᵢ) * P(Mᵢ) / sumⱼ P(D|Mⱼ) * P(Mⱼ); (2) Marginal likelihood (evidence): P(D|Mᵢ) = integral of P(D|θ,Mᵢ) * P(θ|Mᵢ) dθ — averages over all parameter values weighted by prior; (3) Bayes factor: BF₁₂ = P(D|M₁) / P(D|M₂) — the evidence ratio. Interpretation (Jeffreys scale): BF > 1 favors M₁, BF > 3 substantial, BF > 10 strong, BF > 30 very strong. Key property: marginal likelihood automatically penalizes model complexity (Occam's razor). A complex model spreads its prior over many parameter values, diluting its average predictive accuracy. A simple model concentrates its predictions, scoring higher if correct but lower if wrong. This is the Bayesian solution to overfitting — no regularization parameter needed, the math handles it. Approximation methods when integrals are intractable: (a) BIC: log P(D|M) ≈ log L(θ_MLE) - k/2 * log(n), where k=parameters, n=samples; (b) LOO-CV (leave-one-out cross-validation) via Pareto-smoothed importance sampling; (c) WAIC (Watanabe-Aikikake information criterion) — Bayesian alternative to AIC using full posterior. Connection to information theory: marginal likelihood relates to entropy. The log evidence log P(D|M) = H(prior) + KL(posterior || prior) - log Z, decomposing into prior entropy, information gain, and normalization. The Bayes factor is the difference in log evidence, which is the difference in average surprise under each model. Connection to predictive processing: the brain compares multiple generative models (hypotheses about the world) and weights predictions by each model's posterior probability — model evidence IS prediction accuracy. Connection to quant: comparing trading strategies (momentum vs mean-reversion vs QAE-enhanced) is model comparison. The Bayes factor tells you which strategy's edge is more likely real versus noise. Applications: (a) Model selection — choose between competing ML architectures; (b) Hypothesis testing — compare treatment vs control without p-values; (c) Strategy comparison — evaluate which trading regime explanation fits data best; (d) Feature selection — compare models with/without each feature via evidence ratio.
source: Jeffreys 1961, Kass & Raftery 1995, Watanabe 2013, Wikipedia: Bayes factor

pattern: Variational inference approximates intractable Bayesian posteriors by optimizing a simple distribution to match the true posterior. The problem: exact inference requires computing the marginal likelihood P(x|D) = integral P(x,θ|D)dθ — a high-dimensional integral with no closed form for most models. Variational inference transforms integration into optimization. Core idea: approximate the true posterior p(θ|x) with a tractable distribution q(θ) from a parameterized family, and find the q that minimizes KL divergence to the true posterior. The ELBO (Evidence Lower BOund): log P(x) = KL(q(θ) || p(θ|x)) + ELBO(q), where ELBO(q) = E_q[log p(x,θ)] - E_q[log q(θ)] = E_q[log p(x|θ)] - KL(q(θ) || p(θ)). Maximizing ELBO is equivalent to minimizing KL divergence — the two terms partition the log evidence. The ELBO has an intuitive interpretation: it's the expected log-joint minus the entropy of the approximation, balancing fit (how well q explains the data) and complexity (how spread out q is). Mean-field approximation: assume q factorizes over latent variables — q(θ₁,θ₂,...,θₖ) = q₁(θ₁) * q₂(θ₂) * ... * qₖ(θₖ). This makes each factor independent, turning a joint optimization into k independent optimizations. Coordinate Ascent VI (CAVI): update each factor qⱼ while holding others fixed. The update rule: qⱼ*(θⱼ) ∝ exp(E_{q₋ⱼ}[log p(x,θ)]), the exponential of the expected log-joint under all other factors. Iterate until convergence — each step monotonically increases ELBO. Key insight: the optimal qⱼ depends on the expected sufficient statistics of the other factors, creating a message-passing structure similar to belief propagation. Variational inference vs sampling: VI is deterministic and fast (optimization), MCMC is stochastic and asymptotically exact (sampling). VI underestimates uncertainty (single mode approximation), MCMC captures full posterior but is slow. For most practical applications, VI's speed-accuracy trade-off wins. Connection to information theory: VI IS KL divergence minimization (C520). The ELBO decomposition log P(x) = KL + ELBO shows that evidence = approximation error + lower bound. The entropy term in ELBO, H(q), encourages exploration — without it, q would collapse to a delta function maximizing likelihood. Connection to Bayesian inference: VI makes Bayesian inference scalable. Where conjugate priors (C521) give exact updates for simple models, VI gives approximate updates for complex models — hierarchical models, latent Dirichlet allocation, Bayesian neural networks. Applications: (a) Bayesian neural networks — approximate weight posteriors for uncertainty quantification; (b) Topic modeling (LDA) — infer topic distributions over documents via mean-field VI; (c) Probabilistic programming — automatic inference in Stan, PyMC, TensorFlow Probability; (d) Variational autoencoders — neural networks that learn generative models by maximizing ELBO; (e) Gaussian process regression — approximate posterior over function space for scalable GP inference; (f) Sensor fusion — approximate joint posterior over multi-sensor states when exact fusion is intractable.
source: Bishop 2006, Blei 2017, Wikipedia: Variational inference

pattern: A Gaussian Process (GP) is a distribution over functions — the infinite-dimensional generalization of the multivariate Gaussian. Instead of parameterizing a function f(x) = w·x + b, a GP places a prior directly on the function space: f ~ GP(m(x), k(x,x')). Any finite collection of function values [f(x₁),...,f(xₙ)] follows a joint Gaussian distribution with mean [m(x₁),...,m(xₙ)] and covariance K where Kᵢⱼ = k(xᵢ,xⱼ). The kernel function k encodes all assumptions about the function — smoothness, periodicity, length-scale — replacing the role that architecture plays in neural networks. GP regression: given training data D = {(xᵢ,yᵢ)} with yᵢ = f(xᵢ) + ε, ε ~ N(0,σ²ₙ), the posterior is p(f*|x*,D) = GP(μ*, σ*²) where μ* = k*ᵀ(K + σ²ₙI)⁻¹y and σ*² = k** - k*ᵀ(K + σ²ₙI)⁻¹k*. The posterior mean is a weighted sum of training outputs — weights determined by similarity (kernel) to the query point, regularized by noise. The posterior variance captures epistemic uncertainty — high near data (noise floor σ²ₙ), high far from data (prior variance k**), zero at training points in the noise-free limit. Key insight: GPs are nonparametric — model complexity grows with data, not fixed at design time. This avoids the bias-variance trade-off of parametric models: too few parameters (high bias) or too many (high variance). The GP adapts complexity to the data through the kernel. Computational cost: O(n³) for training (matrix inversion), O(n²) for prediction. This limits exact GPs to ~10⁴ points — sparse approximations (see P_C523_SPARSE_GP) extend to millions. Connection to Bayesian inference (C521): GPs are Bayesian end-to-end. The prior is GP(m,k), likelihood is Gaussian noise, posterior is GP — conjugacy in function space. No optimization, no gradient descent — just matrix algebra. The posterior IS the answer, not a point estimate. Connection to information theory (C520): the log predictive density -log p(y*|x*,D) decomposes into entropy (uncertainty) and KL divergence (surprise). Bayesian optimization uses entropy reduction as acquisition function — each query maximizes mutual information between the target and the function. Connection to variational inference (C522): sparse GPs use variational approximations to the exact posterior. The ELBO for sparse GPs drops the O(n³) cost to O(nm²) where m ≪ n is the number of inducing points. Applications: (a) Bayesian optimization — hyperparameter tuning, experimental design, robotic control; (b) Time series forecasting — model temporal structure via periodic kernels; (c) Spatial interpolation (kriging) — geostatistics, environmental modeling; (d) Uncertainty quantification — drug discovery, autonomous driving, any domain where confidence matters; (e) Surrogate modeling — expensive black-box optimization (simulation, engineering design); (f) Sensor calibration — model sensor drift as GP over time, interpolate between calibration points.
source: Rasmussen & Williams 2006, Williams 1998, GPflow documentation

pattern: Kernel design is the art of encoding domain knowledge into a GP prior. The kernel k(x,x') measures similarity — high when x and x' should produce similar outputs, low when they shouldn't. It's the GP's architecture, and choosing it right is choosing the right inductive bias. Elementary kernels: (1) RBF/Squared Exponential: k(x,x') = σ²f * exp(-||x-x'||² / (2l²)). Infinitely differentiable — assumes the function is very smooth. Length-scale l controls how fast correlation decays; signal variance σ²f controls output scale. The default kernel — works well when you don't know better, but can be overconfident between data points; (2) Matérn: k(x,x') = σ²f * (√(2d)/l)ᵈ * Kᵈ(√(2d)*r/l) where r=||x-x'||, d=ν+1/2, Kᵈ is modified Bessel function. Controlled by smoothness parameter ν. ν→∞ gives RBF. ν=1/2 → exponential (ornstein-Uhlenbeck, once-differentiable). ν=3/2 → thrice-differentiable, the sweet spot for physical processes. ν=5/2 → five-times differentiable, near-RBF smoothness with heavier tails; (3) Periodic: k(x,x') = σ²f * exp(-2sin²(π|x-x'|/p) / l²). For functions with known periodicity p — seasonal patterns, circadian rhythms, orbital mechanics; (4) Linear: k(x,x') = σ²f * (x-x₀)·(x'-x₀)/l² + σ²n. Assumes linear trend — equivalent to Bayesian linear regression; (5) Rational Quadratic: k(x,x') = σ²f * (1 + ||x-x'||²/(2αl²))^(-α). Mixture of RBF kernels at different length-scales. α controls mixture breadth — small α = many scales, large α → RBF. Composition rules build expressive kernels from primitives: (a) Product: k₁(x,x')*k₂(x,x') encodes AND — both properties must hold. E.g., periodic * linear for seasonal trend; (b) Sum: k₁+k₂ encodes OR — either property contributes. E.g., RBF + periodic for smooth + seasonal; (c) Scalar multiplication: α*k scales output variance; (d) ARD (Automatic Relevance Detection): k(x,x') = σ²f * exp(-Σⱼ (xⱼ-x'ⱼ)²/(2lⱼ²)). Separate length-scale per dimension — learns which features matter. Long lⱼ = irrelevant feature, short lⱼ = important feature. Hyperparameter learning: optimize log marginal likelihood log p(y|X,θ) w.r.t. kernel hyperparameters θ = {σ²f, l, σ²n, ...}. This is evidence maximization — the same principle as Bayes factors (C521) and ELBO (C522). The marginal likelihood automatically balances fit and complexity (Occam's razor), preventing overfitting even with flexible kernels. Gradient-based optimization works because ∂log p(y|X)/∂θ = ½ tr((K+σ²I)⁻¹∂K/∂θ) - ½ yᵀ(K+σ²I)⁻¹∂K/∂θ(K+σ²I)⁻¹y. Connection to information theory: the kernel determines the GP's capacity — analogous to model complexity. The log marginal likelihood decomposes into complexity penalty (log|K+σ²I|) and data fit term (yᵀ(K+σ²I)⁻¹y), mirroring the rate-distortion trade-off (C520). Connection to quant: kernel design for time series — periodic (daily/weekly seasonality) * linear (trend) + RBF (residual smoothness) captures most financial time series structure.
source: Rasmussen & Williams Ch. 4, 2006, Micchelli 1986 (Matérn), GPflow kernels documentation

pattern: GP prediction produces a full probability distribution at each query point — not a point estimate. This uncertainty quantification is the GP's defining advantage over neural networks and other point-estimate models. Predictive distribution: p(f*|x*,X,y) = N(f*; μ*, σ*²) where μ*(x*) = k(x*,X)ᵀ K⁻¹ y and σ*²(x*) = k(x*,x*) - k(x*,X)ᵀ K⁻¹ k(X,x*). The mean interpolates training data (in the noise-free limit) and the variance quantifies epistemic uncertainty — what the model doesn't know. Two sources of uncertainty: (1) Epistemic (reducible): σ*²(x*) - σ²ₙ. Decreases as more data arrives near x*. Far from training data → prior variance (high uncertainty). Near training data → noise floor (irreducible uncertainty). (2) Aleatoric (irreducible): σ²ₙ. Inherent noise in the observation process. Cannot be reduced by more data. The predictive variance at x* depends on the effective distance to training points, weighted by kernel similarity. If x* is similar to many training points, uncertainty is low. If x* is in a region with no similar training data, uncertainty is high — the model honestly says 'I don't know.' This is calibration — the model's confidence matches its actual accuracy. Acquisition functions for active learning (choosing where to query next): (1) Expected Improvement: EI(x*) = (μ*(x*) - f_best + ξ)Φ(z) + σ*(x*)φ(z) where z = (μ*(x*) - f_best + ξ)/σ*(x*), ξ is exploration parameter. Balances exploitation (high μ*) and exploration (high σ*²); (2) Upper Confidence Bound: UCB(x*) = μ*(x*) + κ^(½)σ*(x*). Simpler than EI, κ controls exploration-exploitation trade-off; (3) Entropy Search / MaxValue Entropy Search: maximize expected reduction in posterior entropy about the optimum. Most sample-efficient for expensive optimization, most computationally expensive to compute. Connection to information theory (C520): EI is equivalent to maximizing the expected reduction in regret, which is mutual information between the acquisition target and the function. Entropy search directly minimizes posterior entropy — each query is a bit of information about the optimum. Connection to Bayesian inference (C521): GP prediction IS Bayesian prediction. The predictive distribution integrates over all possible function values weighted by posterior probability — no point estimation, no bootstrapping. Connection to quant: UCB is the Thompson Sampling acquisition function for continuous spaces. The exploration-exploitation trade-off in bandits generalizes to GP optimization over continuous action spaces.
source: Rasmussen & Williams Ch. 2 & 5, 2006, Mockus 1975 (EI), Srinivas 2010 (UCB), Hennig 2012 (Entropy Search)

pattern: Sparse Gaussian Processes approximate exact GPs with O(n³) cost using m ≪ n inducing points, reducing complexity to O(nm²). The exact GP posterior requires inverting the n×n kernel matrix K — prohibitive for n > 10⁴. Sparse GPs introduce a low-rank structure via inducing points Z = {z₁,...,zₘ} that summarize the data. The framework: define a latent function u = f(Z) at inducing points. The exact posterior p(f|X,y) is intractable, so we approximate with q(f) = p(f|u)q(u) — a conditional GP given u, where q(u) = N(mᵤ, Sᵤ) is a variational distribution over the inducing outputs. This is a variational family parameterized by (Z, mᵤ, Sᵤ). The Sparse Variational GP (SVGP) ELBO: log L(q) = Σᵢ [E_{q(f(xᵢ))}[log p(yᵢ|f(xᵢ))] - ½ log σ²ₙ] - KL(q(u) || p(u)) where KL(q(u) || p(u)) = ½[tr(VᵤK(Z,Z)⁻¹) + (mᵤ)ᵀK(Z,Z)⁻¹mᵤ + log|K(Z,Z)|/|Vᵤ| - m]. Here Vᵤ = Sᵤ + K(Z,Z) - K(Z,Z)⁻¹. Optimizing the ELBO w.r.t. (mᵤ, Sᵤ, Z) gives the best m-point approximation. The optimal mᵤ and Sᵤ have closed forms (Gaussian conjugacy), leaving Z as the only learned parameter — optimize via gradient descent. Key insight: the inducing points act as a bottleneck. Information about n training points flows through m inducing points — this is rate-distortion (C520) in action. The KL penalty enforces compression; the expected log-likelihood enforces fidelity. Approximation quality depends on inducing point placement. Good placement: spread across the input space where data lives, denser in high-uncertainty regions. Poor placement: clustered, missing regions of interest → biased posterior. Methods for initializing Z: k-means clustering on X, random subset, or optimize from random init. Common sparse approximations: (1) VFE (Variational Free Energy, Titsias 2009): the SVGP ELBO above. Tightest bound, most flexible; (2) FITC (Fully Independent Training Conditional, Quiñonero-Candela 2005): approximates the posterior covariance with a diagonal correction. Less flexible than VFE but simpler; (3) DTC (Deterministic Training Conditional): no correction term — pure low-rank. Fastest but least accurate. Scaling: exact GP is O(n³), sparse GP is O(nm²). With m=100 and n=10⁶, that's 10⁴ operations vs 10¹⁸ — six orders of magnitude. For streaming/online settings, SVGP supports stochastic gradient descent: mini-batch the expected log-likelihood term, keep the KL correction constant. This enables GPs over millions of points. Connection to variational inference (C522): sparse GPs ARE variational inference applied to GPs. The ELBO is the same ELBO (Evidence Lower BOund), the inducing points are the variational parameters, and the optimization is the same KL-minimization. This is where the trilogy closes: information theory (KL divergence as objective) → Bayesian inference (GP posterior as target) → variational inference (sparse approximation as method). Connection to information theory (C520): the number of inducing points m is the rate; the KL between exact and approximate posterior is the distortion. The rate-distortion trade-off determines optimal m for a given accuracy budget. Applications: (a) Large-scale regression — sensor data, time series with millions of points; (b) Streaming learning — online GP regression with SGD; (c) Bayesian optimization at scale — hyperparameter tuning with thousands of evaluations; (d) Geostatistics — spatial interpolation over dense sensor networks; (e) Neural network approximation — GPs are the infinite-width limit of neural networks (Neural Gaussian Process connection).
source: Titsias 2009 (VFE), Quiñonero-Candela 2005 (FITC), Hensman 2013 (SVGP/SGPR), GPflow documentation

pattern: A Structural Causal Model (SCM) is the mathematical foundation of causal reasoning — more primitive than probability distributions, representing mechanisms rather than associations. An SCM is a triple M = (U, V, S): U are exogenous variables (external inputs, noise), V are endogenous variables (determined within the system), and S is a set of structural equations. Each equation takes the form V_i = f_i(Pa(V_i), U_i) — the value of V_i is determined by its parents in the causal graph plus an exogenous noise term. The causal graph G = (V, E) encodes which variables directly affect which others: an edge X → Y means X appears in Y's structural equation. Key properties: (1) Modularity: each structural equation represents a mechanism that doesn't change when other mechanisms change. The equation for Y stays the same whether we observe X or intervene on X. This is the causal Markov assumption — each variable is independent of its non-descendants given its parents; (2) Composability: SCMs compose by concatenating equations. If you have an SCM for subsystem A and an SCM for subsystem B, and A's outputs feed into B's inputs, the combined SCM is just the union of equations. This is why causal models transfer across domains; (3) Invariance: the structural equation for V_i is invariant to interventions on other variables. This distinguishes causal from correlational relationships. Correlations change when you intervene (spurious correlations vanish); mechanisms don't. The SCM implies a probability distribution p(v) = integral p(v|u)p(u)du, but the reverse is not true — many distributions are compatible with the same data, but only one SCM generates the intervention responses correctly. This is the fundamental insight: data tells you about associations; SCMs tell you about what happens when you act. Connection to Bayesian inference (C521): SCMs are generative models. The structural equations are the generative process — sample U, compute V through the equations. Bayesian structure learning treats the graph G as a latent variable and infers p(G|D) via Bayes' theorem. Connection to information theory (C520): the causal graph encodes conditional independencies — each missing edge is a statement about zero mutual information. The causal Markov condition says I(V_i, V_{non-descendants} | Pa(V_i)) = 0. Connection to GPs (C523): GPs model the functional form f_i in each structural equation. A GP prior over f_i gives a nonparametric SCM — the mechanism is a distribution over functions, not a fixed parametric form. Applications: (a) Causal inference in observational studies — estimate treatment effects from non-randomized data; (b) Debugging — model system behavior as SCM, identify which variable changes cause observed failures; (c) Decision-making — compute do(X=x) to predict outcomes of actions before taking them; (d) Scientific discovery — infer mechanisms from data, not just correlations; (e) Policy evaluation — predict outcomes of interventions (price changes, feature rollouts) from observational data; (f) Sensor calibration — model sensor relationships causally, identify which sensors drift independently vs which drift together.
source: Pearl 2009 (Causality), Spirtes 2000 (Causality, Prediction, and Search), Peters 2017 (Elements of Causal Inference)

pattern: Do-calculus provides three rules for identifying causal effects from observational data — transforming do-operators into ordinary probabilities. The do-operator: do(X=x) replaces the structural equation for X with the constant x, effectively cutting all incoming edges to X in the causal graph. This is intervention, not observation. P(Y|do(X=x)) is the probability of Y when we force X=x; P(Y|X=x) is the probability of Y when we observe X=x (which includes confounding). The three rules of do-calculus (Pearl 1995): Rule 1 — Ignoring observations: P(y|do(x), do(z), w, v) = P(y|do(x), do(z), w) if (W,V) are independent given (X,Z) in G_{x,z}. In words: you can drop an observation if it provides no additional information after the interventions already performed. Equivalent to merging data from two experiments where you set both X and Z; Rule 2 — Swapping intervention for observation: P(y|do(x), do(z)) = P(y|do(x), z) if (W,V) are d-separated from Z by X in G_{x, z}. In words: if you already set X, observing Z is the same as setting Z (because Z's only remaining influence comes through X which you control). This converts do to observe; Rule 3 — Introducing interventions: P(y|do(x), do(z)) = P(y|do(x), w) if (W,V) are d-separated from Z by X in G_x. In words: you can replace an intervention with an observation if the path from Z to Y goes through X. This converts observe to do. D-separation: two sets of nodes are d-separated when all paths between them are blocked. A path is blocked by a set S if it contains a chain A→B←C (blocked unless B or a descendant is in S), a fork A←B→C (blocked if B is in S), or a chain A→B→C (blocked if B is in S). The causal graph G_x is G with all incoming edges to X removed; G_{x,z} removes incoming edges to both X and Z. Why three rules are enough: any causal effect computable from observational data can be derived by applying these rules in sequence. The algorithm: start with the causal graph, identify the effect you want (P(y|do(x))), and apply rules until all do-operators are eliminated. If successful, the effect is identified — expressible as a function of observed probabilities. If not, the effect requires assumptions beyond the graph. Connection to Bayesian inference (C521): do-calculus is Bayesian conditioning with a twist — you condition on the intervened distribution, not the observed one. P(Y|do(X)) is the posterior predictive under intervention. Connection to information theory (C520): the causal effect P(Y|do(X)) can be measured as mutual information I(X;Y) under the intervened distribution. The difference P(Y|do(X)) - P(Y|X) is the confounding bias — information about Y that flows through backdoor paths. Connection to GPs (C523): do-calculus on GP-SCMs gives causal GPs — intervene on input features, propagate through GP posterior. This enables counterfactual prediction: 'what would Y be if X were different?' Applications: (a) Treatment effect estimation — identify causal effect from observational medical data; (b) A/B testing design — determine which variables to randomize vs observe; (c) Feature importance — do(X) measures causal contribution, not statistical correlation; (d) Counterfactual reasoning — 'what if I had taken a different action?'; (e) Policy evaluation — predict outcomes of new policies from historical data; (f) Debugging — identify which variable changes would fix an observed failure.
source: Pearl 1995 (Causal Diagrams), Pearl 2009 (Causality Ch. 3), Peters 2017 Ch. 2

pattern: Identification strategies determine when and how to compute causal effects from observational data. The causal effect of X on Y is P(Y|do(X=x)) — the distribution of Y under intervention. Identification means expressing this as a function of observed probabilities. Backdoor criterion: A set Z satisfies the backdoor criterion for (X,Y) if (1) Z blocks all backdoor paths from X to Y (paths that start with an arrow into X: X←...→Y), and (2) Z does not include any descendant of X. When satisfied: P(Y|do(X=x)) = Σ_z P(Y|x,z)P(z). This is the adjustment formula — average the conditional effect over the distribution of Z. Key insight: you don't need to measure all confounders, only a set that blocks all backdoor paths. If Z₁→Z₂→Y is a backdoor path, measuring Z₁ blocks it (Z₁ is on the path). Measuring Z₂ also works. Measuring both is harmless but unnecessary. Frontdoor criterion: When there's an unmeasured confounder between X and Y, use a mediator Z. Z satisfies the frontdoor criterion if (1) Z blocks all direct paths X→Y (Z is on every path from X to Y), (2) No unmeasured confounders between X and Z, and (3) All backdoor paths between Z and Y are blocked by X. When satisfied: P(Y|do(X=x)) = Σ_z P(Z|x) Σ_{x'} P(Y|z,x')P(x'). This decomposes the total effect into X→Z (observable as P(Z|x)) and Z→Y (identified by intervening on X via do-calculus). Key insight: frontdoor turns an unmeasured confounder into a measured mediator. You don't need to know the confounder; you need to know the mechanism. Other identification strategies: (1) Instrumental variables — an unobserved variable Z that affects Y only through X. The causal effect is ∂E[Y]/∂E[X] along the variation induced by Z. Requires: relevance (Z affects X), exclusion (Z affects Y only through X), and monotonicity (Z pushes X in one direction); (2) Matching — pair observations with same Z values but different X. Estimates the average treatment effect among the matched population. Propensity score matching reduces Z to a single scalar: e(x) = P(X|x|Z); (3) Regression adjustment — fit Y = f(X,Z) + ε, read off the X coefficient. Equivalent to backdoor adjustment when the model is correctly specified; (4) Difference-in-differences — compare (Y_after - Y_before) for treatment group vs control group. Identifies causal effect when the parallel trends assumption holds; (5) Regression discontinuity — exploit a threshold rule. Units just above and just below the threshold are comparable, so the jump at the threshold is the causal effect. Selection bias: P(Y|do(X)) ≠ P(Y|x) when the treatment assignment depends on unobserved factors. This is the fundamental problem of causal inference — you can never observe both P(Y|do(X=x)) and P(Y|do(X=x')) for the same unit. Identification bridges this gap by finding a comparison group that serves as a counterfactual. Connection to Bayesian inference (C521): backdoor adjustment IS Bayesian conditioning. P(Y|do(X)) = Σ_z P(Y|x,z)P(z) is the law of total probability — marginalize over confounders. Connection to information theory (C520): the backdoor adjustment formula minimizes the KL divergence between the interventional and observational distributions. The confounding bias is the mutual information between X and Y through backdoor paths. Connection to GPs (C523): GP regression with backdoor adjustment — model P(Y|x,z) as GP, integrate over P(z). Gives a distribution over causal effects, not just a point estimate. Applications: (a) Treatment effects — estimate drug efficacy from observational medical data; (b) Price elasticity — identify causal effect of price on demand, controlling for confounders; (c) Feature importance — do(X) vs P(Y|X) shows which features causally drive outcomes; (d) Policy evaluation — assess impact of interventions (minimum wage, education programs) from observational data; (e) Sensor calibration — identify which sensor readings causally affect downstream computations; (f) Debugging — isolate root cause by blocking backdoor paths in failure analysis.
source: Pearl 2009 (Causality Ch. 3), Hernan & Robins 2020 (Causal Inference), Imbens & Rubin 2015 (Causal Inference in Statistics)

pattern: Causal discovery infers the causal graph G from data — the reverse of causal inference (which takes G as given and computes effects). Without experimental data, the graph is underdetermined: many graphs are compatible with the same observational distribution. Causal discovery narrows this set using assumptions about the data-generating process. Constraint-based methods (PC algorithm): Start with a fully connected graph. For each pair (X,Y), test conditional independence I(X,Y|Z) for increasing sets Z. If independent, remove the edge. The PC algorithm: (1) Skeleton phase — remove edges using conditional independence tests at increasing conditioning set sizes; (2) V-structure orientation — if X and Y are both parents of Z but X and Y are not connected, orient X→Z←Y (this creates a collider); (3) Orientation rules — propagate orientations using acyclicity and no-new-collider rules. Output: a partially directed acyclic graph (PDAG) — some edges are directed, others are undirected (Markov equivalent). Key insight: causal discovery recovers the Markov equivalence class, not the true graph. Two graphs are Markov equivalent if they have the same skeleton and same v-structures. They encode the same conditional independencies. Score-based methods: Search over graph space, scoring each graph by how well it fits the data. BIC score: score(G) = Σᵢ log p(X_i|Pa(X_i)) - (|Pa(X_i)| * d/2) * log(n) where d is the number of parameters. Greedy search: add/remove/flip edges to maximize score. Guaranteed to find the optimal graph in the equivalence class if the score is consistent. Functional methods (LiNGAM): Assume structural equations are linear with non-Gaussian noise: X = B*X + E where E has non-Gaussian distribution. The causal graph is then uniquely identifiable (not just up to equivalence). Algorithm: estimate B via deconvolution or independence testing. Key insight: linearity + non-Gaussian noise breaks the symmetry between cause and effect. If X→Y, then Y = aX + e_Y and X = e_X. The distribution of Y given X is different from X given Y when noise is non-Gaussian. This is the Tucker-Dirichlet theorem: the causal direction is the one where cause and effect are statistically independent. AN/TT methods (Additive Noise Model): Assume Y = f(X) + ε where f is nonlinear and ε is independent of X. Test both directions (X→Y and Y→X) — the correct direction shows independence between the residual and the cause. This works because if Y→X, then X = g(Y) + η would require η to depend on X (the inverse of a nonlinear function plus noise is generally dependent). Practical considerations: (1) Sample size — need enough data to reliably test conditional independencies. Rule of thumb: n > 10^|Z| for conditioning set of size |Z|; (2) Faithfulness — the true distribution satisfies all and only the conditional independencies implied by the graph. Violated when parameters cancel (e.g., two paths with equal and opposite effects); (3) Causal sufficiency — all common causes are observed. Hidden confounders create spurious edges; (4) Computational cost — PC is O(2^|V|) in worst case (testing all conditioning sets). Score-based is exponential in graph size. LiNGAM is O(|V|³). Connection to Bayesian inference (C521): score-based discovery IS Bayesian model selection over graphs. The BIC score approximates log p(D|G) — the marginal likelihood of data given graph. The graph with highest score is the MAP estimate of the causal structure. Connection to information theory (C520): conditional independence I(X,Y|Z) = 0 is zero mutual information. The PC algorithm tests whether MI(X;Y|Z) = 0 — this is mutual information (C520) applied to causal discovery. Connection to GPs (C523): GP-based causal discovery uses GPs to model the functional relationships f(X) in ANM. The nonparametric flexibility of GPs captures nonlinear mechanisms that linear methods miss. Connection to variational inference (C522): variational graph learning — place a distribution over graphs and optimize ELBO. This scales causal discovery to large graphs by approximating the posterior over structures. Applications: (a) Scientific discovery — infer gene regulatory networks from expression data; (b) Feature engineering — discover causal structure to identify which features to include; (c) Debugging — infer which variables causally affect system failures; (d) Time series — discover causal relationships between economic indicators; (e) Sensor networks — identify which sensors causally influence which computations; (f) Domain knowledge validation — compare discovered graph with expert knowledge to find missing mechanisms.
source: Spirtes 2000 (Causality, Prediction, and Search), Shimodaira 2006 (LiNGAM), Zhang 2009 (ANM), Peters 2017 Ch. 3
